en: Preface to the Illustrated Map of the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Garden: This monastery and vihāra was constructed as a separate *saṃghārāma*.

There are great causes and conditions for this, which preclude my from citing the sūtras and vinaya at length to clarify the foundations of this temple. It covers eighty *qǐng* of land and consists of one hundred and twenty courtyards (*vihāra*).
From east to west it is nearly ten *lǐ*, and from south to north it is over seven hundred *bù*. As it has been recently transmitted.
It is said:
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, Sudatta and Jeta jointly established the Jetavana Grove; this is recorded in the sūtras.
According to what has been heard previously, two hundred years have passed since then.
This was precisely the thirty-first year of King Ping, the thirteenth sovereign of the Zhou dynasty in this land.
Why was it that [the city] was completely consumed by fire?
It was because Prince Jeta cherished and protected this garden.
Sudatta pressed him to purchase the land, refusing to spare even the expenditure of gold;
the Prince’s feelings of stinginess were so intense that he deeply regretted his offer,
yet Sudatta remained firm in his resolve, utterly unshakable.
Seeing that he was not stingy with his gold and rejoiced in making offerings,
the Prince told the elder,
"I shall build the temple myself; you need not assist me."
Sudatta did not permit it.
The Prince made a vow:
"If the tree becomes golden, I shall not need [anything else] to provide for my offerings."
Later, even if it were to fall into ruin, he prayed that the tree would grow back again;
just as it was about to be burned, the buildings were completely destroyed, yet the tree that had been planted remained no different than it was originally.
This was when Sudatta was still an ordinary man.
Selling meat to acquire wealth is a base occupation;
though one may emerge wealthy, one constantly prays for famine and scarcity.
Even if one attains great riches, the wealth stems from a defiled mind.
Because of this, the temple he built ultimately met with total destruction by fire.
Although Prince Ruci’s power of pure mind and his cultivation of meritorious deeds were deficient, his inconceivable nature remains beyond measure.
Four hundred years later, there was a king named Yuga;
his power was not even one-tenth of what it had been based on the land.
After a thousand or more years, it was reduced to ashes by bandits.
Thirteen years later, there was a king named Ṣaṭśīrṣaka who,
following the previous example, rebuilt the palace with magnificent structures adorned entirely with jewels.
One hundred years later, an evil king destroyed it and turned it into a place for slaughtering people.
The Four Heavenly Kings and the Dragon King Sāgara were incensed;
they crushed those who had destroyed [the image] with great stones,
so that for ninety years the land remained desolate and devoid of human inhabitants.
The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven commanded his second son to descend to the human realm to act as a guide.
Furthermore, he fashioned exquisite ornaments from earth-flowers;
this continued for one hundred and fifty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Heavenly King Māra incinerated [the land].
This corresponds to the twenty-ninth year of the reign of Emperor Xian during the late Han dynasty in this land of China.
Having already used these events to verify the Manifestation of the Honored One (Xianzong), [he continued:]
Later, during the reigns of Emperors He, An, Huan, and Ling, travelers coming and going from the Western Regions arrived in succession;
they witnessed the construction of the Heavenly King’s temple and the circumstances by which the Jetavana Grove flourished once again.
Although there were some who followed later, their foundations have by this day fallen into ruin and desolation alone.
Regarding the name of the monastery, Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma, according to the monastic records, it possesses ten names in total.
First, it is called a temple (sa).
Second, it is called a dwelling for pure abiding (śuddhapratiśaraṇa).
Third, it is called a communal dwelling for the Dharma (dharmasamāna-śālā).
The fourth is the supramundane dwelling;
the fifth is the vihāra;
the sixth is the pure grove.
Seventh is the Vajra Pure Land;
eighth is the Site of Enlightenment of Quiescence;
ninth is the Place of Remote Seclusion.
The tenth is "the place of intimacy.
These ten names above explain the characteristics based on the sutras;
each has its own significance as set forth in those scriptures.
Now, based upon various sūtras, this garden was first constructed.
Its ground measures over eighty *qīng* in circumference from south to north, and it extends eastward for some five or six *lǐ* to the south of Śrāvastī;
however, when checking various biographies and records, the measurements in *li* and *bu* sometimes differ slightly.
It is truly so that after first arising, one creates prolonged service rather than spontaneity;
those who act according to the seasons are merely recorded as they appear,
which causes scholars of narrow views to dwell therein for a time.
Although there are many theories regarding the location of the site of the Buddha’s enlightenment, it is certain to be south of the city;
this can be understood through comparison. There are two large courtyards.
The western courtyard is where the monks reside and is named Daochang (Dharma-Field).
Alternatively, the foundation of the Vajramaṇḍala may rise from the ground with separate steps and stairways;
niches on all four sides shall each enshrine spirits and monsters to guard this courtyard.
The great wall has three tiers;
it is approximately twenty feet high and provided with a projecting eave.
The supporting beams and rafters are joined together, and the vermilion and white plaster gleam against one another.
According to the Monastic Code (Sīgào),
the outermost enclosure wall represents the external protection of the Three Refuges.
The innermost court has walls whose interior and exterior surfaces depict the mirror-like aspect of the causes and effects of the Three Jewels;
this inner court is elevated above the outer court.
The five chi in height symbolize that the causes and fruits of the Triple Gem transcend the five realms of existence. Furthermore,
regarding the various numbers of Buddha halls, Dharma shrines, and Sangha monasteries,
as well as their architectural layouts and decorative motifs, each follows its own distinct and exemplary conventions.
There are separate seats for the Brahma Kings and the Heavenly Kings,
and distinct chambers for the wild spirits and hungry ghosts;
all are fully prepared and attended to with the eight offerings and the six seasonal sacrifices.
The giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma, as well as the practice of eating little at appropriate times versus eating more, each have their own specific purpose.
The details are as found in those extensive texts.
This great monastery complex has three gates aligned along its three sides.
The northern gate was not opened.
According to Master Yu’s *Record of Sacred Sites*,
two gates— the northeast and the east— were opened at the monastery.
Surrounding the Jeta Grove Monastery are eighteen temples.
Furthermore, according to the *Sìgào* (Monastery Records),
it is said that this single site of the Jeta Grove has four gates that penetrate through one another.
The cross-shaped layout corresponds to the current diagram.
Regarding the fact that there is no gate in the north, a detailed examination of the matters reveals that the architectural systems for the front and rear were each distinct,
having been constructed according to the times and based on what was heard and seen.
Arranging them in this manner need not be considered strange;
this diagram and its commentary represent the original layout of the Golden Cord (Suvarṇasūtra).
On the southern side are three gates, with the main gate at the center.
As for the five-bay, three-storied high tower that outshines all others,
it was built by Prince Jeta.
These three stories symbolize the three gates of emptiness (śūnyatā).
This clarifies the three emptinesses of the Buddha-dharma.
Taking the entry into the principles of the Buddha as the fundamental origin, the robe was established as the primary tenet;
thus, the three layers were instituted to represent the three emptinesses.
Outside the gate, the canal water flows beneath a flying bridge that spans it from north to south; it also has five lanes.
The variety of its carvings and decorations is truly beyond anything human.
The two gates to the east and west have three stories each, as described above, and both consist of three bays.
Outside the gate, three flying bridges extend straight in; beyond them are forest trees that circle it in purity.
Upon reaching the flowering trees at the three sides, those who meet [the deity] enter with a heart of profound reverence.
The side gates of the left and right courtyards of the Great Central Gate face one another across the water, where trees grow in dense clusters.
The eastern gate of the main courtyard aligns with the central axis, providing thoroughfare from east to west;
this gate is exceptionally tall and grand, surpassing all other courtyards.
Stacked one above the other in twelve tiers,
with seventeen gates spanning the ground,
its marvelous adornments stand preeminent, towering over the empty wilderness.
When people from the four quarters, whether monastics or laypeople, first arrive to pay their respects, they do not dare to face north;
only after having passed through many such gates within the monastery do they finally approach the presence [of the Master].
According to the temple records,
this grand and magnificent gate symbolizes the place where one first enters the Way through faith.
Its multi-storied pavilion is adorned with white paintings on both the interior and exterior, depicting the image of Mahābrahmā and the image of Śakra-devendra.
Regarding the images of the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the King of Men, the Great Demon King, and the Dragon Kings:
the reason their forms and features are depicted is to signify that,
like shadows and echoes, they universally protect the maintenance and sustenance of the Triple Gem.
The state of the western gate of the Great Courtyard has not been heard of;
because its functions reside in impermanence, its dimensions remain unmanifest.
To the east of the main gate, there are seven separate courtyards.
On the southern side, the first courtyard to the west is named the Courtyard of the Lay Bodhisattvas from Other Lands.
This courtyard has a gate opening to the north, and within it is a hall filled with flowering trees.
Whenever laypeople or bodhisattvas from other regions come from afar to pay their respects, they first stay here;
only later do they see the Buddha. Within this courtyard is a crystal lion.
The King of Tuṣita fashioned it with his own hands;
it was about the size of a fist.
When the time came, it emitted a wondrous sound from its mouth like that of the jīvaṃjīvaka bird.
Within the sounds [of the Dharma], eighty thousand pāramitās are expounded.
Upon hearing this teaching, the bodhisattvas ascend to the stages (bhūmi).
Every year on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, [they do so].
The men and women of Śrāvastī each held incense and flowers and came to listen to the sound of the Dharma;
even the jīvañjīvaka birds, the sons of the garuḍas, the mandarin ducks, and the phoenixes all came together to attend.
Some humans and various birds attained the first fruit [of the path],
while others entered the Dharma-eye of the Mahāyāna and attained purity.
Next, to the north of the small alley was a courtyard named the Courtyard of Bodhisattvas from Other Directions.
The gate is secured with a crossbar and opens to the south; its inner halls and rooms, as well as the groves of trees, are as described before.
Within it stands a sturdy mallet, and there is a copper dragon fashioned by the Great General Vaiśravaṇa.
The stone lotus flower blooms when the sun rises and closes when the sun sets.
When it is time for it to close, all its petals move as if stirred by a breeze;
the dragon then utters a sound, and the *karmadāna* hears this voice.
Thereupon, the ghaṇṭā was struck.
To the southeast of the western courtyard,
there was a courtyard named the Bhikṣuṇī-āgamana-śikṣā-prārthanā-vihāra (the Courtyard for the Arrival of Bhikṣuṇīs and the Request for Instruction).
One gate faces north toward the street of the eastern gate;
one gate faces east, and within it there is a hall and trees,
as in the middle of the western courtyard.
On the new and full moons each month, when the bhikṣuṇīs come to request instruction, they reside in this monastery.
There is a *kṣatriya* pillar about thirty feet high,
constructed by an asura king.
At the top of that land, there was a phoenix with a copper bell in its beak.
Whenever a bhikṣuṇī approached, the bell would ring of its own accord;
if she did not act in accordance with the Dharma, the bell would sound discordantly.
There was an instance of diligent practice involving the use of foul language for the purpose of rebuking;
he then raised his voice to offer praise and spoke of the various dharmas of the six perfections.
Next, there was a courtyard to the north of the street named the "Instruction Courtyard for Bhikṣuṇīs."
Inside there is a hall with a gate facing south that opens outward;
one gate opens to the east as in the description of the previous courtyard.
Every month, on two occasions, nuns come to receive instruction and admonition.
To the northwest of the front [courtyard] is a large compound called the Courtyard of the Buddhas of Other Directions;
they come here from time to time for the sake of manifesting their transformations.
Within, it was filled with groves, ponds, flowers, and trees.
The two gates to the east and west opened facing the main street.
Mahābrahmā Devendra manifested twelve square stone slabs.
Upon the pure and radiant seat sat the Buddha;
therein was a celestial drum of mani-jewels,
which would sound of its own accord when the time arrived.
It was created by the Naga King Vasuki;
its sound is heard from afar,
reaching as far down as the depths of the waters and as high as the Peak of Existence.
Those in the hells, upon hearing this, shall be freed from suffering and be reborn in the heavens; those who have entered the fruition shall likewise attain it.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle shall reach the Great Vehicle, and those who have first resolved their minds for enlightenment shall enter the seventh stage.
To the north of the Buddha Courtyard Lane, there are further two courtyards.
The courtyard on the western side is named the Buddha Incense Storehouse Courtyard;
its gate faces west and opens onto the main street.
Among these, the one held by the Celestial Youth is the next eastern courtyard, named the Courtyard of the Various Immortals;
its gate opens to the south, and the halls and trees are lush and abundant.
Within it is a section of three thousand kinds of celestial music made of the seven precious gems; each is held aloft by a person made of the seven precious gems.
When the sages assemble, these instruments sound of their own accord, playing celestial melodies.
When the Buddha entered the Immortals’ Grove to preach the Dharma,
the beings made of the seven treasures played melodies on the Six Perfections and the Four Noble Truths,
causing the mountains of pride of the immortals with the five supernatural powers to collapse.
Some attained the three fruits [of the śrāvaka path], while others entered the first bhūmi; these cannot be described in detail.
This joy of the śrāvakas occurred throughout one four-continent world-system during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, when it was produced by the Great Seer Mārīcī on Mount Gandhamādana.
After the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, Mañjuśrī brought it to Mount Qingling.
When Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, he took it to the Jetavana Monastery.
Upon the Tathāgata’s final extinction, this music spontaneously flew away to the Vajra Cave on Mount Qingling.
The seven upper courtyards are all situated to the east of the main gate and to the west of the eastern gate.
Within them, channels and streams intersect and flow through one another, remaining clear and pristine.
Furthermore, the expansive views are so captivating that one forgets all weariness and fatigue while gazing upward in admiration.
The southern face of the eastern gate is as described for the three preceding layers.
Directly to the north, spanning the bridge, is a *wutoumen* (arched gateway).
One proceeds straight through five successive gates before finally reaching the central street.
To the east of the eastern gate, nine courtyards are divided;
first, to the south and west,
there is one courtyard named the Courtyard of the Great Brahmā King.
Within the two gates, east and west, there are twelve celestial conch shells.
When the Brahmās assemble, they first halt here;
they are adorned with garments of liberation and constant robes.
When he wished to approach the presence of the Buddha, the conch shell sounded of its own accord;
its sound reached throughout the trichiliocosm.
When the Brahma King wished to inquire about the six perfections and the four noble truths, [the conch sounded].
The conch shell emitted its sound as soon as it was blown;
all who heard the sound gathered at the Buddha’s location.
Furthermore, within the courtyard there was a jade pond.
Within the pond were golden lotuses;
in their centers sat thirteen celestial youths holding conch shells and buds,
which remained closed until the Buddha arrived, at which point they blossomed.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahābrahmā Devendra was about to return to the heavens.
To the east of that, there is a courtyard named the Courtyard of Knowing the Time.
Its gate opens to the west, facing all the other courtyards.
When the *karmadāna* observes the signs and contemplates, he is within this court.
Inside it, there is a courtyard with eaves and beams;
further within, there is a golden Mount Sumeru surrounded by the waters of the ocean.
The wondrous things within these mountains cannot be fully described.
Above, there is a golden city with towers and watchtowers made of white silver and the seven precious gems.
It is over three *zhang* in height.
It was constructed by the third son of Mahābrahmādeva.
It has four corners with four pavilions, totaling twelve gates on its four sides.
Above each of the four gates there is likewise a tower.
Within each of these four towers resides a precious being;
when the time comes, they emerge to repel the enemy, striking a drum.
Upon this city wall, twelve men were already stationed in the open air;
each holding a white fly-whisk, they proclaimed that noon had arrived.
The southern gate then opened, and the horse emerged from within.
As the hours pass, the gates contract and close accordingly with the twelve periods of the day;
the emergence and disappearance of the beasts follows this same pattern.
During the night, there are many other people who perform the watch-duty, each clearly distinguished from the others.
When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, the mountains shook and sounds issued forth;
all activities of the time were suspended,
and the jewel-like people wept, some even breaking their hands [in grief].
Twelve years after his parinirvāṇa,
the Great Brahmā King gathered it back to heaven;
when Maitreya descends to be born, it shall return once more to its original place.
To the north of the two halls is a large courtyard.
This large courtyard is further divided into four sections.
The first section on the southwestern side is named the Hall of Offerings from Māra.
The gate opens toward the east.
When Mārathevatī first descended, she first entered this inner courtyard,
where there was a bell made of seven-edged, seven-cornered maṇi jewels, with a capacity of three hundred thousand *jia*.
At the time of the Great Assembly of Humans and Devas at Jetavana,
the bhikṣu Aśvajit had the māra-son Priyadarśana strike the bell;
its sound reached throughout the great trichiliocosm, and the Māras heard it.
He immediately led eight hundred billion celestial sons of Māra;
furthermore, there were another ten billion māra kings who also arrived at the same time,
holding up jewels to offer to the Buddha.
All those in the hells shall immediately be freed from suffering.
This bell-vessel was fashioned by an ancient Buddha prior to the Kalpa of the Constellations (*Nakṣatra*).
After that Buddha passed into *nirvāṇa*, the nāgas took it back into the ocean.
Next to the east is another courtyard named the Great Buddha Image Courtyard.
Its gate opens toward the west.
Within it, the magnificent halls, jeweled walls, flower gardens, fruit groves, ponds, and forests are such that words cannot fully describe them.
To the north of these two halls, there were another two halls.
The one immediately to the west was named the Hall of the Dragon King;
its gate opened toward the east, and within it stood a large central hall.
Furthermore, inside there was a single lapis lazuli vase;
within the vase were seven excellent golden cocks that would crow as soon as a dragon arrived,
their sound heard across three hundred million *li*.
When the Dragon King Sāgara arrived, seven roosters crowed together;
when other dragons arrived, only one rooster would crow.
The interior and exterior of his vase were transparently clear.
The golden pheasants are shaped like this mountain pheasant, and their calls sound like the music of a sheng pipe.
When the dragons hear them, their anger subsides.
As the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, all the pheasants flew away.
When Kāśyapa convened the council, the two chickens returned;
when Ānanda entered nirvāṇa, they flew away and did not return.
In former days, the great nāga kings who came to pay homage to the Buddha were the first to arrive at this courtyard.
He cast off his dragon form and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Furthermore, there were three tiers of jade chimes;
when the dragons assembled in great numbers, the bhikṣu Pūrṇa would have the dragon prince Maṇas strike them.
The sound reached throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Within it, dragon kings each brought precious objects to offer to the Buddha.
This gong was made by the Dragon King Sāgara during the Constellation Kalpa.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the nāgas took it back into their palace.
Next to the east is another place called the Hall of the *Kumbhīra* Court;
this court has its gate opening toward the west.
All the flowering trees within the courtyard are as described before.
To the north of that is a large courtyard called the Layman’s Courtyard (Kusha-jin-in).
Its gate opens southward onto an alley, and in its center stands a hall.
Whenever laypeople and householders first enter the monastery,
they first stop at this courtyard where there are four bronze bells,
each weighing three thousand *jin*. Their shape is like those cast during the reign of King Zhou of the Zhou dynasty in this land.
On all four sides, there are images in relief made of white silver.
Furthermore, there are images depicting the Tathāgata as a prince,
such as his wrestling with a horse and other such feats.
The nose of the bell is cast in the shape of a copper dragon.
An immortal is mounted upon its back,
holding a golden mallet in his hand and striking downward at the bell.
For the śrāvakas throughout Jambudvīpa,
during the four seasons, he emits a voice like the sound of a celestial lute;
therein he preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the śrāvakas.
In summer, it is like the sound of heavenly pipes;
therein he expounds the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and the Dharma of the Four Truths for Bodhisattvas.
During the two seasons of autumn and winter, it is like the sound of heavenly thunder.
The text describes the Dharma of the Buddhas' initial attainment of enlightenment.
Regarding these bells, each of the Four Great Heavenly Kings fashioned one;
they were hidden beneath the ground of the main Jeta Grove monastery by spirits, to be revealed only when the karmic conditions were met.
Then, all the laypeople who heard the sound of the bell immediately understood the essential points of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata;
those who had attained the three fruits in spring attained the forty minds prior to the stages (bhūmi) in summer.
In autumn and winter, one realizes the second bhūmi.
To the north of the lay devotees' courtyard, there are two separate courtyards;
the one on the western side is named the Courtyard of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Its gate opens toward the south onto the alleyway.
This great bodhisattva was at that time situated within it.
Inside was a Buddha hall, fully adorned with all manner of ornaments.
In the flower ponds, groves, and bamboo thickets, devas and humans gather;
there, they propagate the sublime Dharma to deliver those with whom they have a karmic affinity.
There is a great bell tower as well as a great drum with a silver mouth and a golden face.
Mañjuśrī expounded the six perfections for the sake of the bodhisattvas; this drum likewise proclaimed the six perfections.
It is the same with all other dharmas.
This drum came from the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) to provide offerings here.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he returned to the heavens and caused his voice to resound throughout the trichiliocosm;
those in the hells who heard it were freed from suffering and attained liberation.
To the east of the Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Hall is a building named the Monks’ Treasury Hall.
Its gate opens onto a south-facing alley.
All the wealth, treasures, and requisites of the monastic community are stored within it, from the top down to this point.
To the east of the main gate and south of the great lane, and again to the west of the main gate, there are seven courtyards.
The first, located at the southernmost eastern edge, is the Courtyard of the Four Noble Truths of the Bodhisattva.
Within was a great hall with its doors facing north; groves and ponds filled the courtyard.
There, various bodhisattvas expounded upon the Four Noble Truths in detail, their discourse both broad and concise, treating the principles of existence and emptiness, bondage and liberation.
The convergence of all ordinary beings and sages, as well as the flow and obstruction of their paths, is gathered therein.
The various monastic schools follow this precedent, so it is not described in detail here.
The monastery possesses three tiers of golden bells.
The nose has the form of nine dragons;
when the time comes, the dragon mouths emit much cloud-vapor.
The bell then sounds of itself, its tone like a celestial lute, heard for twenty li.
This was a gift fashioned by the Naga King Vasuki.
Long ago, when the Buddha Krakucchanda was practicing the path as a bodhisattva,
the Buddha’s own master-craftsman created it through his own inspired ingenuity.
"I vow that in the future I shall attain a golden body,
and may this bell forever serve as an offering to all Buddhas.
Next, to the north of the small alley, there is a courtyard named the Courtyard of the Bodhisattva’s Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
The gates face south, and the courtyard and hall are adorned with trees; within, there is no bell.
There is a golden son, like a small Japanese boy, who at the appointed time produces a sound like that of a celestial *kōng-hou* (lute).
The sounds he uttered— explaining the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, impermanence, suffering, and emptiness for the Bodhisattvas—
pervaded the city of Śrāvastī.
When he wished to stop speaking, he would cover his mouth with an object.
The sound then ceased;
this was created by the Naga King Manasvin for his son when the Tathagata was about to enter parinirvana.
Blood gushed from the eyes of the dog as he cried out:
"How marvelous! World-Honored One, in three months' time you shall enter parinirvāṇa.
This was the very first proclamation of the news.
When humans and devas heard this, they all felt sorrow and lamentation.
Next was the Hall of the Four Truths for Bodhisattvas.
To the west of that hall, there was yet another hall.
This is named the Prajñāpāramitā Twelve Links of Dependent Origination Courtyard.
To its east stands the Bodhisattva Four Noble Truths Courtyard;
the trees and halls are identical to those [of the former], and the gate faces north toward the alleyway.
Within it is a golden bell shaped like three ox horns;
its small ends are joined together, and atop them is a *k'un-lun* knob fashioned as the "nose" of the golden bell.
When a gentle breeze blows upon it at the proper time, its sound is heard for eight *li*.
This was constructed by King Vaiśravaṇa during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month, the bell is able to recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* of Kāśyapa Buddha,
and the fourfold assembly gathers to listen.
Next, to the north of the narrow alley, there is a courtyard named the Courtyard of the Four Truths of the Pratyekabuddhas;
its gate opens to the south.
Persons of the pratyekabuddha disposition delight in hearing the two dharmas.
The Buddha taught according to their individual capacities and dispositions.
Within it was a great hall, groves, and ponds, all pure and serene—
a place of profound seclusion and retreat.
There is a bronze cauldron-shaped bell;
when struck by a person, its sound is heard for a hundred li.
It was unearthed during the excavation of the ground when this monastery was being constructed.
It was bestowed by the Earth Deity Sthāvarāputra.
To the north of these four courtyards is a large courtyard named the Courtyard for Questioning the Dharma by Those Beyond Training (aśaikṣa); its gate faces north toward the lane.
The great arhats who had come to inquire about the Dharma gathered there together.
There was a great Buddha hall that extended as far as the eye could see;
it was lofty and prominent, with groves and ponds interspersed, which all who beheld it admired.
They revere the Buddha’s teachings as eternal.
There is only a single bamboo bell,
its shape resembling that of a gong.
It was originally fashioned by a Gandharva king;
the bell's clapper had a golden knob,
which he held in his own hand as he struck it.
When the time came, he struck it, and the sound was like that of a human lute; the music ceased within the courtyard.
Within the sounds, the twelve divisions of the scriptures were expounded, and every spring when the flowers bloomed, all the youths of Śrāvastī would come to view and listen.
While enjoying the pleasures of the five desires, they hear the Dharma and attain its fruits.
Furthermore, to the north of the narrow alley, it is divided into two courtyards from east to west.
On the western side, one courtyard is named the Courtyard for Students to Reside and Listen to the Dharma.
The gate faces south onto an alleyway.
The halls, ponds, and groves are reflected therein, no different from what was described above.
Great Brahmā Deva fashioned a celestial kōng-hóu (lute).
Pure silver was placed within this monastery;
when the time came, the Trāyastriṃśa gods blew sounds that reached as far as the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana heaven,
